newsitem.title: UK: Grobbelaar the clown has not forgotten pain of war.
newsitem.headline: Grobbelaar the clown has not forgotten pain of war.

text.p: Zimbabwean goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar, cleared on Friday of charges of receiving cash to fix matches, found it hard to be any more earnest in court than he has been during his reign as the uncontested "clown prince" of English soccer.

Grobbelaar, who won five championships with Liverpool, has at his peak been the great eccentric of the English game, renowned both for his athletic saves and the horrendous unforced errors which cost his club dear in several important European competitions.

But behind the flamboyance lay the nightmare of his national service in the Rhodesian army, when as a 17-year-old he took part in the protracted conflict which ended with Zimbabwean independence in 1980.
Down the years, some marvelled and others cringed at the born showman's juggling and gymnastic antics. He outraged traditionalists and occasionally panicked his defenders with sudden forays upfield.

When his case went for re-trial after the jury failed to reach a verdict in a first trial earlier this year, the judge warned Grobbelaar that he would not put up with a repeat of his persistent joking with his co-defendants.
Grobbelaar, 39, behaved himself at his second trial -- but could not resist turning up in a succession of highly colourful outfits.

Grobbelaar now plays for second division Plymouth Argyle after a spell at premier league Southampton. He has not let the trial affect his nerves on the pitch, and is due to turn out for Zimbabwe on Sunday in a World Cup qualifying game against Togo.
When obliged to wear a mask to protect a face injury two seasons ago when playing for Southampton, he typically chose one in the colours of the Zimbabwean flag.
But for Grobbelaar, the flag was more than just flamboyance, and inevitably evoked memories of his traumatic army service.
"I saw my best friends killed in the bush and I killed people myself. I still have nightmares in which I hear the screams and see the frightened faces," he wrote.
Perhaps this has given Grobbelaar his determination to rise above the occasional deadly earnestness of what is only a game.
"If war teaches you anything it is an appreciation of being alive. I will never apologise for laughing at life and enjoying my soccer," he said.
During a 13-year career at Liverpool, he won league championship medals in 1982, 1983, 1984, 1986 and 1988 and shared in League Cup success in 1982, 1983 and 1984.
Grobbelaar also collected English F.A. Cup medals in 1986 and 1989 and helped Liverpool to the European Cup in 1984.
There is no doubt Liverpool's brilliant record in the 1980s owed much to Grobbelaar's often inspired reading of the game.

Among his many admirers is former England manager Bobby Robson, who was quoted as saying that "had Bruce been English he would, without question, have won international honours during my time as England's manager".
"Bruce isn't simply an outstanding goalkeeper, blessed with incredible agility. He also gives his team an extra defender. He reads the game like an outfield player."
Liverpool signed Grobbelaar for 250,000 pounds ($400,000) in 1981 from Vancouver Whitecaps in Canada after he had started his English career with lowly Crewe in 1979.
Bruce David Grobbelaar was born on October 6, 1957 in what was then Rhodesia. He is married with two young children. ($ = 0.628 British Pounds)
